title: The pandemic paradox: The consequences of COVID‐19 on domestic violence

body.text:
seen people's day-to-day life drastically altered. These changes are essential to beat coronavirus and protect health systems (UK Home Office, 2020). However, there are unintended, negative consequences. As the virus continues to spread across the world, it brings with it multiple new stresses, including physical and psychological health risks, isolation and loneliness, the closure of many schools and businesses, economic vulnerability and job losses. Through all of that, children and their mothers are particularly vulnerable (End Violence against Children, 2020) to the risk of domestic violence.

Domestic violence refers to a range of violations that happen within a domestic space. It is a broad term that encompasses intimate partner violence (IPV), a form of abuse that is perpetrated by a current or ex-partner. In this editorial, we talk about "domestic violence" because this is the term used most often in the media. It is important to clarify though that we are mainly referring to IPV and its impact on children who live with or are exposed to IPV between adults. We also focus mainly on women, because they are disproportionately affected by domestic violence; however, we recognise that domestic abuse happens to men and occurs within same-sex relationships.

It is a matter of just about a week ago where one of us (Bradbury-Jones) was writing another editorial about COVID-19 for the Journal of Clinical Nursing, reflecting on life in the pandemic (Jackson et al., 2020). Within that editorial, we raised the emerging concern as to whether domestic violence rates would rise as a result of the "lockdown" that is being imposed by many countries across the globe.

Although these measures vary, to some degree, in their timing and severity, they generally require that people stay at home and only leave for an essential reason such as buying food, collecting medication or carrying out a key worker role. At the time of writing this first editorial, the concern was expressed as speculation, a questioning as to whether it might happen. Within such a short time span, there is clear evidence that we need to speculate no more. Domestic violence rates are rising, and they are rising fast.

Experience in New Zealand and internationally has shown that family violence (including IPV, child abuse and elder abuse) and sexual violence can escalate during and after large-scale disasters or crises (NZFVC, 2020). Around the world, as communities have gone into lockdown to stop the spread of coronavirus, the mass efforts to save lives have put women in abusive relationships more at risk.

A very recent article published in The Guardian (2020) reported on how the surge of domestic violence cases is a pattern being repeated globally. Reporting from several different countries, the article highlighted alarming figures, for example a rise of 40% or 50% in Brazil.

In one region of Spain, the government claimed that calls to its helpline had risen by 20% in the first few days of the confinement period and in Cyprus, calls to a similar hotline rose 30% in the week after the country confirmed its first case of coronavirus. In the UK, Refuge, one of the leading domestic abuse organisations reported that calls to the UK Domestic Violence Helpline increased by 25% in the seven days following the announcement of tighter social distancing and lockdown measures by the government. During the same period, there was a 150% increase in visits to the Refuge website (BBC, 2020). Governments across the globe are imposing necessary draconian measures to try to level the curve of the virus and to delay its peak. In the UK where we both live and work, we have listened to what has become a well-rehearsed mantra: Stay Home; Protect the National Health Service (NHS); Save Lives. We use this editorial to propose the pandemic paradox, to unravel and problematise these measures in terms of what they mean for those who are living and surviving abusive relationships.

Let us start with staying at home. Home is not always a safe place to live; in fact, for adults and children living in situations of domestic and familial violence, home is often the space where physical, psychological and sexual abuse occurs. This is because home can be a place where dynamics of power can be distorted and subverted by those who abuse, often without scrutiny from anyone "outside" the couple, or the family unit. In the COVID-19 crisis, the exhortation to "stay at home" therefore has major implications for those adults and children already living with someone who is abusive or controlling. Stringent restrictions on movement shut off avenues of escape, help-seeking and ways of coping for victim-survivors.

Restrictive measures are also likely to play into the hands of people who abuse through tactics of control, surveillance and coercion. This is partly because what goes in within people's homes-and, critically, within their family and intimate relationships-take place "behind closed doors" and out of the view, in a literal sense, of other people. Unintentionally, lockdown measures may therefore grant people who abuse greater freedom to act without scrutiny or consequence.

Social norms and attitudes that suggest there is a "sanctity" to family life-to home, in a social rather than physical sense-can also make it difficult for people to speak out about, let alone leave, abusive situations as a result of feelings of shame and embarrassment. During the COVID-19 crisis, it is therefore important to think critically about idealised representations of home and family and to make it possible for people to talk about, and where possible take action to counter abusive and controlling family life. Asking people directly, on repeated occasions, about whether they consistently feel safe at home is one way of doing this; however, it is also important that people asking this question have the time and emotional resources to listen and respond to the often-subtle ways that people indicate they are scared and unsafe.

As regards protecting health, social and therapeutic services, of course there has been considerable focus on front-line staff, directly relevant to dealing with the novel coronavirus. Nurses and health professionals are clearly at the forefront of the response to COVID-19 and we stand with those underlining the need to meet, as a basic requirement, health professionals' physical, practical and emotional needs during and after the immediate impact of the pandemic. It is vital that health services are protected and resourced. It is also vital, however, that we continue and where necessary increase support to the services who work alongside health and avoid tendencies to pit services against one another in practical or moral terms. Services working alongside health include the advocates, therapists and helpline practitioners working in specialist domestic and sexual violence services in the voluntary sector. These organisations provide an array of services, including but not limited to refuge accommodation, independent advocacy and peer support and mentoring services.

Their independence is often highly valued by victim-survivors, many of whom may have had difficult experiences with institutions such as the police or social services. During the COVID-19 crisis, these services are more crucial than ever. They provide support and care to victim-survivors experiencing immediate danger and distress.

Thus, it is critical that governments across the world enable these services to remain open. This means ensuring that voluntary sector practitioners can access personal protective equipment, be paid in full and be supported to care for their own families whilst working.

It also means finding new solutions, including increasing capacity for helpline services and running targeted campaigns, alongside specialist services, about discrete ways that victim-survivors can contact the emergency services without alerting their abuser (Independent Office for Police Conduct, 2019). For people already accessing crisis and therapeutics services, the use of phone support and online technologies to provide advice and counselling is welcomed. However, it is also important to recognise that victim-survivors may not have access to these mechanisms because of control tactics used by an abusive partner, or more simply, because they cannot afford them.

This underlines the need to provide different types of support and to recognise that many people will simply not be able to access help or care whilst social restrictions are in place and this will have an impact on their safety, health and well-being now and in the longer term.

In terms of saving lives, one of the most serious manifestations of intimate partner and familial abuse is domestic homicide. In the UK, approximately two women are killed every week by their current or ex-partner. During the COVID-19 pandemic, reports have emerged of an apparent increase in domestic homicides in a number of affected countries. In March 2020, Spain (a country that has been particularly hard hit by the pandemic) saw its first domestic violence fatality just 5 days following lockdown; a woman was murdered by her husband in front of their children in Valencia. There is also emerging evidence of an increased number of domestic homicides in the UK since the lockdown restrictions were enacted (Ingala . At this early stage of the pandemic, it is too early to verify whether the increased reporting of these deaths represents an actual rise in domestic homicide rates or increased media attention. However, it is important to highlight that reported cases are of violence are known to be a small percentage of actual incidents.

Moreover, the emerging homicide numbers underline the serious and potentially devastating unintended consequences of the pandemic for victim-survivors of abuse.

At the time of writing, we are grappling, like everyone else, with the myriad, often deeply worrying effects of this novel coronavirus.

Seeking to stem its spread, safeguard our health systems and, critically, best protect those with health vulnerabilities that put them at risk of life-limiting or life-ending illness, it has been necessary to alter social behaviours like never before and for governments to alter radically, the extent to which they intervene into our private lives and behaviours. We raise concerns about the needs and experiences of victim-survivors of domestic violence as a way of drawing attention to some of the unfortunate and troubling paradoxes of social distancing and isolation measures, not in opposition to them.

We do so because the voices and needs of victim-survivors are too often over-looked and under-represented in some parts of the media and within policy and political spheres. We also raise these issues because there are actions that may help to mitigate the additional risks that COVID-19, and its attendant social and economic effects, may have on victim-survivors. National and local governments can, for example, take action now in terms of protecting and supporting services that provide crisis and therapeutic support to victim-survivors. However, it is also by being aware of and, where possible, reaching out to those who may be affected by domestic violence that we can support one another, whether in our personal or professional lives. This pandemic creates a paradox as regards staying safe at home and it is one to which we should all pay attention. Governments across the globe have called upon us all to play our individual part in tackling COVID-19 by staying at home, but a critical mindfulness of what this means for many women and children is also important.

title: Optimizing Road Flow with Genetic Algorithms and Deep Learning

body.text:
INTRODUCTION

Estimating road capacity is a foundational task in traffic control, representing the maximum number of vehicles that can pass through a specific point within a designated period, given prevailing roadway and traffic conditions (Reilly, 1997). Traditional capacity assessment relies on static, guideline-based models that estimate capacity from fixed geometric and topological road attributes (e.g., lanes, widths, segment type, speed limits). Consequently, capacity is treated as a near-constant, segment-level value, largely independent of network conditions and real-time traffic fluctuations. 

However, such static models lack the flexibility needed to reflect dynamic traffic states and typically do not capture interactions among road segments. In real-world networks, traffic conditions are inherently coupled: changing the effective capacity of one segment can shift bottlenecks, modify route choices, and propagate congestion upstream and downstream, thereby affecting speeds and flows throughout the network. This motivates a network-wide optimization perspective, in which segment capacities are not treated as isolated parameters but as decision variables that should be selected based on their global impact on overall network performance. 

In this study, we propose a data-driven optimization framework that operationalizes this system-level view of capacity. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and deep learning enable accurate prediction of traffic dynamics under varying flow configurations. Combined with network-wide optimization, these predictions allow segment capacities to be determined through a global optimization process that maximizes a predefined network level objective while enforcing safety and operational constraints. In this formulation, capacity is not merely a descriptive engineering metric, but a controllable variable that can be tuned to achieve desirable system-level outcomes. 

Beyond improving traffic prediction and control, this perspective opens the door to future traffic management paradigms in which optimized capacities serve as a foundation for coordinated access regulation mechanisms. In particular, capacity values derived from system-level optimization can, in principle, enable structured and incentive-aware allocation schemes, such as market-based or auction-inspired mechanisms, that regulate vehicle entry into congestible road segments in a manner that promotes ef-ficiency, safety, and congestion avoidance. While the present work focuses on the optimization and modeling layer, it establishes a necessary computational and conceptual basis for such mechanisms by reframing capacity as an outcome of network-wide optimization rather than a fixed, exogenous constraint. 

Our approach addresses the limitations of static models by enabling continuous, dynamic capacity assessment that adapts to evolving traffic patterns. Specifically, we propose a two-stage framework that integrates traffic-speed prediction with network-wide flow optimization to improve road utilization and traffic efficiency under real-time conditions. 

The first stage of our methodology focuses on Traffic Speed Prediction. To forecast traffic speed across the network, we develop a suite of spatiotemporal deep learning models for multivariate exogenous regression, which predict future speeds by learning patterns from current and historical traffic flow data. We employ multiple architectures, i.e., Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Bidirectional LSTM (Bi-LSTM), and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), in order to capture both temporal patterns and network structure. These models produce accurate, actionable speed forecasts that account for flow-speed interdependence and serve as inputs to the optimization stage. 

The second stage performs network-wide flow optimization using a Genetic Algorithm (GA) to determine segment capacities as decision variables. Rather than optimizing each road segment in isolation, the GA searches for flow configurations that improve overall network performance while accounting for network interactions. The learned flow-speed relationship is used as a surrogate evaluator: for each candidate solution, the prediction model estimates the resulting speeds, which are then incorporated into the fitness function. In addition, predicted speed-flow information can guide the generation of new offspring during crossover, steering the search toward feasible and efficient capacity configurations. 

Our methodology addresses a central challenge in traffic control: the spatial interdependence of road networks. Conditions in one area often cascade to neighboring segments, creating ripple effects that require a network-wide perspective. This interdependence makes it difficult to optimize individual segments without accounting for system-level impacts. Our framework addresses this challenge by simultaneously handling multiple interacting road segments at the network level. As a result, it supports more effective capacity-oriented decisions and enhances the robustness and adaptability of traffic management systems. 

The contributions of this study are as follows: We train and validate the framework on real-world flow and speed measurements from operational road networks, enabling capacity-oriented decisions grounded in observed traffic behavior rather than synthetic assumptions. • General Framework for Multi-Variable Optimization Using Available Big Data: By integrating machine learning predictions with genetic algorithms, we provide a scalable framework for optimizing multiple interacting variables, with an OOD safeguard that prevents unrealistic solutions. 

Our approach advances network-wide road flow management by enabling data-driven, real-time optimization of both speed and flow, providing transportation planners with greater precision and control than traditional static models. Beyond traffic applications, the proposed hybrid framework offers a general AIdriven optimization methodology that can be adapted to other complex, data-rich domains, such as energy grid management and supply chain logistics, supporting next-generation intelligent decision-support systems. 

LITERATURE REVIEW

Capacity Estimation

Road capacity refers to the number of vehicles that can pass a given point during a specific period under prevailing roadway, traffic and control conditions (Reilly, 1997). There are many factors that affect road capacity such as external conditions including the weather, visibility and road lighting (Chung et al., 2006). Road density also affects capacity: under congestion, far fewer vehicles can enter without worsening traffic than the nominal capacity would suggest (Chen et al., 2001). 

Traditionally, the estimation of capacity done by transportation engineers is often based on guides such as the Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) (Reilly, 1997) or the bureau of public roads (BPR) link function. Table 1 outlines the HCM Level of Service (LOS) criteria for basic freeway segments, with Free-Flow Speed (FFS), minimum speed, and maximum flow rate as essential components for evaluating traffic performance. Free-Flow Speed (FFS) represents the ideal, unconstrained speed that vehicles can maintain on a road segment in optimal conditions, without interference from other vehicles, traffic control devices, or adverse environmental factors. Minimum speed within each LOS category refers to the lowest average speed that vehicles are likely to achieve under increasing levels of congestion. This metric helps quantify the reduction in travel speed as traffic density rises, where lower LOS levels (like D and E) correspond to significant speed reductions. Maximum service flow rate (pc/h/ln) represents the highest volume of vehicles that can pass through a lane per hour while still maintaining the designated LOS. As traffic density and congestion increase, the maximum flow rate adjusts to reflect the capacity that each LOS level can sustain. 

Table 1: Level-of-Service (LOS) criteria for basic freeway segments (Exhibit 23-2) at a free-flow speed (FFS) of 100 km/h, adapted from (Reilly, 1997). The Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) guidelines have been widely criticized for overestimating road capacity and failing to account for interdependencies within road networks (Li and Laurence, 2015;Moreno, 2020;Khaksar et al., 2024). HCM provides generalized, guideline-based capacity estimates under idealized conditions, typically treating capacity as a fixed value determined by factors such as Free Flow Speed (FFS) and maximum flow rate. While effective for analyzing isolated segments, this static perspective often overlooks road-specific characteristics and interactions with adjacent segments, limiting its ability to capture dynamic, network-wide effects under fluctuating traffic conditions. 

Criteria

To address these limitations, recent research has increasingly explored data-driven approaches for estimating link capacity and link performance. Huo et al. (Huo et al., 2022) propose a domain-informed deeplearning framework that embeds the classical BPR link performance function within a neural architecture to jointly estimate link capacity and calibrate the BPR parameters. Their model is trained end-to-end using observable travel times, thereby alleviating the lack of ground-truth capacity labels. Using Vissim-simulated data, the approach substantially outperforms conventional handbook-style capacity adjustment methods; however, the evaluation relies on simulation rather than real-world observations. Yin et al. (Yin et al., 2022) infer capacity indirectly through simulation by running SUMO under different free-flow speed (FFS) settings and estimating link capacity from the resulting speed-flow relationship (fundamental diagram). Assuming a triangular FD, they define capacity as the maximum attained flow for each FFS scenario. Based on these simulated capacity estimates across a range of FFS values, they fit a logarithmic capacity-FFS relationship and show that it differs from standard HCM freeway-based formulas. 

Classical machine learning has also been used to model traffic states from observed features. In our previous work (Lewis et al., 2024), we compared multiple learning methods (linear regression, K-nearest neighbors (KNN), decision trees, neural networks, and ensemble models) for predicting traffic speed from flow and additional road-related features. While that study trained models at the level of individual road segments using segment-specific attributes and then estimated, for each segment separately, the flow level that maximizes throughput, it did not capture network-wide interactions. In the current study, we propose a data-driven, macro-level optimization approach that combines genetic algorithms with machine learning to explicitly account for interdependencies across the network. Rather than imposing rigid per-link capacity limits, our method optimizes traffic flows holistically using real traffic data and adapts to interactive effects between segments, enabling real-time adjustments aimed at improving overall network efficiency, reducing congestion, and lowering travel times across interconnected roads. 

In our study, we perform multivariate time-series regression with exogenous (external) inputs. Specifically, given recent observations of traffic flow, the model predicts the traffic speed series. This setting differs from standard univariate forecasting because the target series (speed) is predicted using a different input series (flow). In the context of traffic modeling, it is crucial not only to forecast traffic speed but also to capture how changes in traffic flow affect speed, enabling joint optimization of these variables. While extensive research exists on traffic speed prediction, our findings indicate that relatively few studies focus explicitly on predicting traffic speed as a function of traffic flow, as explored in works such as (Gao et al., 2022). This gap highlights the need for models that account for complex interactions between flow and speed in multivariate time-series prediction. 

Traffic Optimization

Traffic optimization has traditionally focused on traffic signal control, with approaches often leveraging evolutionary algorithms, genetic algorithms, and swarm optimization techniques (Aleksander and Paweł, 2020;Qadri et al., 2020;Jamal et al., 2021). These optimization methods are well-suited for handling the complexities of traffic systems, as evolutionary algorithms mimic natural selection processes, while swarm intelligence algorithms draw inspiration from collective behaviors in nature (Khasawneh and Awasthi, 2023). 

Our study takes a different optimization approach: rather than focusing on traffic signal control, we regulate traffic flow at each road section by limiting vehicle input to improve overall network utility. Using a machine learning model that predicts networkwide speeds from flows, we dynamically adjust flows across the network to reduce congestion and improve efficiency. More broadly, integrating machine learning with optimization offers strong potential for improving combinatorial optimization (CO). ML can provide fast approximations for expensive computations and support data-driven decision policies within iterative algorithms, complementing classical heuristics while preserving feasibility considerations. 

Accordingly, machine learning has been increasingly integrated into meta-heuristic algorithms to enhance performance and efficiency, typically in three main ways (Bengio et al., 2021): 

1. Initialization, where machine learning models, such as clustering algorithms or neural networks, are employed to generate high-quality initial populations, thereby accelerating convergence and improving solution quality (Hassanat et al., 2018). 

2. Fitness score approximation, where surrogate models, often based on Gaussian processes or support vector machines, are used to estimate fitness values of candidate solutions, reducing the computational cost associated with expensive fitness evaluations (Moiz et al., 2018). 

3. Evolution models, where reinforcement learning or other adaptive techniques guide the selection of operators and parameters during the evolutionary process, allowing the algorithm to adapt its search strategy based on the problem landscape. 

Machine learning can augment metaheuristic algorithms by guiding their search. For example, predicting effective crossover points in genetic algorithms or adapting particle updates in particle swarm optimization using past performance. Such hybrid approaches often outperform traditional metaheuristics by combining broad exploration with data-driven, adaptive decisionmaking. (Lodi and Zarpellon, 2017). 

Both spatial and temporal models, such as GNNs and LSTMs, have been used to guide optimization by learning how time and space influence key variables. In particular, GNNs have recently gained traction for combinatorial optimization (Cappart et al., 2023) and have also been applied to traffic optimization (Madadi and de Almeida Correia, 2024), due to their ability to represent relational structure via permutationinvariant, sparse message passing. 

In this study, we propose a general framework for multi-variable optimization that combines machinelearning predictions with genetic algorithms to optimize multiple interacting variables in a scalable and adaptable manner. To improve robustness, we also incorporate mechanisms for mitigating out-ofdistribution (OOD) behavior, reducing the likelihood that the genetic algorithm proposes unrealistic inputs that the prediction model cannot reliably evaluate. 

PROBLEM SETUP

In this study, we examine the trade-off between traffic flow (X) and traffic speed (Y ) as a case study for broader multi-variable optimization problems. When traffic flow (and thus density) becomes too high, vehicle interactions increase, speeds drop, and congestion may emerge, potentially even leading to stop-andgo traffic. Therefore, improving network efficiency requires balancing throughput with acceptable speed levels to avoid congestion and maintain driver satisfaction. 

We consider a traffic network composed of n road segments. Our goal is to determine a well-performing allocation of traffic flows, f 1 , . . . , f n , while accounting for the corresponding speeds, s 1 , . . . , s n . These variables cannot take arbitrary values: both flow and speed are constrained by the physical characteristics of each road segment (e.g., capacity, geometry, and regulations) and by vehicle dynamics. Accordingly, our primary objective is to maximize the overall efficiency of the network while satisfying feasibility constraints on both flow and speed. 

To formalize this, we define a utility function F( f 1 , . . . , f n , s 1 , . . . , s n ) that combines flow and speed in order to evaluate network performance. For example, one may use F = ∑ n i=1 f i s i as a throughput proxy that accounts for both traffic volume and speed across all road segments. 

Since speeds depend on flows, we introduce a predictive model M that maps the vector of flows to the corresponding vector of speeds: 

) where the i-th component [M( f 1 , . . . , f n )] i denotes the predicted speed on road segment i. 

Using this representation, the optimization problem is formulated over the flow decision variables: max 

∀i ∈ {1, . . . , n}. 

(2) 

In practice, the quality of the resulting flow recommendations depends directly on the accuracy of M, since both the objective and the speed-related constraints are evaluated through its predictions. Therefore, a first key challenge is to construct an accurate and efficient model that reliably captures the complex, nonlinear relationship between traffic flow and speed, enabling effective network-level optimization under the defined fitness function. 

Our approach integrates machine-learning-based prediction with optimization to iteratively adjust flow levels and evaluate their system-wide impact. As illustrated in Figure 1, increasing flow generally reduces speed due to congestion effects, yet very low flow leads to under-utilization of the network. Consequently, the optimization objective is to identify an intermediate operating point that balances flow and speed to maximize network efficiency. 

METHODOLOGY

The HCM-proposed maximum-flow/minimum-speed pairs for capacity estimation are limited, as they largely rely on Free-Flow Speed (FFS) to characterize the flow-speed relationship and may overlook roadspecific characteristics. Figure 2 shows, for each road segment in our dataset, the average 90th-percentile flow and its corresponding average speed, highlighting substantial variability even among roads with similar FFS. This visualization demonstrates that each road responds differently to changes in flow, despite having comparable FFS. Some roads exhibit high capacity thresholds, maintaining speeds even at higher flow rates, while others show low capacity thresholds, with speeds declining more rapidly as flow increases. These differences highlight the limitations of using broad guidelines or FFS alone to predict flowspeed relationships, emphasizing the need for more nuanced, road-specific models in traffic management and planning. 

Recall from previous sections that we propose a two-stage, data-driven framework that combines spatio-temporal deep learning with genetic algorithms to optimize traffic flows. A learned surrogate model (LSTM/BiLSTM/GNN) predicts networkwide speeds from candidate flow vectors, enabling fast fitness evaluation and efficient GA-based search for feasible flow configurations under operational constraints. To improve reliability, we mitigate outof-distribution behavior by initializing the population with diverse, realistic samples and enforcing feasibility constraints throughout evolution. As shown in Figure 3, we begin with the original data to generate an initial population of candidate flow configurations. For each candidate, the trained model predicts speeds, and a fitness score is computed from both flow and speed, subject to constraint checks that ensure operational validity. The GA then iteratively applies selection, crossover, and mutation to generate new populations until convergence, yielding an efficient set of per-segment capacity (admissible flow) values. 

Machine Learning Models

Our framework follows a two-stage pipeline: first, we learn traffic-speed dynamics from historical timeseries data using a spatio-temporal predictor. Given the current state, a genetic algorithm then recommends the flow vector for the next time step, while the learned model provides the corresponding speed estimates used to evaluate fitness under the network constraints. 

To capture the relationship between traffic flow and traffic speed, we experimented with several deep learning architectures, each offering distinct modeling capabilities. For temporal modeling, we compared an LSTM and a Bidirectional LSTM across different history window lengths. Both architectures used two recurrent layers (64 and 32 units), with the Bidirectional LSTM processing sequences in both forward and backward directions to capture richer temporal context. We also implemented a Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN) following (Yu et al., 2017), which learns a dynamic adjacency matrix in a spatial layer and couples it with a temporal module (LSTM or BiLSTM), followed by a dense output layer. 

All machine-learning models are trained on the training set, with a held-out validation set used for hyperparameter tuning, early stopping, and model selection. After training, the model is frozen and used during optimization solely as an evaluation function that maps candidate flow configurations to predicted speeds; no further learning or parameter updates are performed. 

Genetic Algorithm-Based Traffic Flow Configuration

In our setting, the goal is not merely to predict speeds or flows, but to determine network-wide flow configurations that maximize overall performance for a given traffic state and objective. Each such configuration constitutes a distinct optimization instance, and optimal solutions may correspond to traffic states that are rarely or never observed in historical data. Consequently, learning system dynamics alone is insufficient, as it does not perform structured search over alternative configurations nor does it explicitly account for optimization objectives and feasibility constraints. 

To address these challenges, we formulate network-wide traffic flow regulation as a highdimensional, constrained optimization task and employ a genetic algorithm as the optimization mechanism. Given a traffic network with many interconnected road segments, the decision variables correspond to the flow values assigned to each segment, resulting in a large and non-linear search space that cannot be exhaustively explored using real observations alone. In this framework, the populations generated by the genetic algorithm represent candidate flow configurations within the admissible optimization space rather than synthetic traffic scenarios. These candidates are evaluated using learned traffic response models and planner-defined constraints, allowing the optimizer to efficiently explore feasible solutions while remaining grounded in realistic traffic dynamics. 

We implemented the genetic algorithm using the DEAP Python library (Fortin et al., 2012). Custom processes were developed by modifying the library's default functions to meet our specific needs, while any standard components not discussed here were handled using DEAP's pre-built functions. 

When combining genetic algorithms with machine learning, we face a distinctive challenge: the genetic algorithm may generate candidate solutions that fall outside the distribution represented in the training data, thereby degrading the predictor's reliability. Such out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs can lead to poor generalization and unstable estimates, since most supervised models are not designed to extrapolate far beyond their training regime (Robey et al., 2020). To mitigate this issue, we incorporate additional safeguards for handling atypical candidates, as described in Sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.3. 

The genetic algorithm implementation comprises four components: initialization from real data to improve generalization, ML-based evaluation of candidate populations, enforcement of planner-defined constraints, and dual fitness objectives that optimize both distance traveled and traffic throughput. We next describe each component in turn. 

Initialization

To mitigate the out-of-distribution issue, the initial population of the genetic algorithm is constructed from the original dataset by randomly sampling observed traffic states. This initialization strategy ensures that the algorithm starts from diverse and representative flow configurations, grounding the search process in realistic regions of the solution space. As a result, the optimization procedure is better aligned with the domain in which the learned models are reliable, thereby reducing the impact of OOD effects during the search. 

Combination with Machine Learning Algorithm

The genetic algorithm generates populations that represent the traffic flow across the entire network. Using the machine learning model, we evaluate these populations to predict the corresponding traffic speed. This dual evaluation allows us to apply different fitness scores that combine both flow and speed, providing a more comprehensive assessment of each solution's performance. By optimizing these fitness scores, we ensure that the generated populations not only maximize flow but also maintain efficient speeds, leading to a more balanced and effective network performance. 

Constraints

The genetic algorithm also allows us to incorporate specific constraints defined by traffic planners, such as maximum and minimum flow, and maximum and minimum speed. Incorporating these constraints ensures that GA generated solutions remain both efficient and compliant with practical and regulatory requirements, allowing planners to retain control over critical parameters and align optimized flows with safety and operational standards. Consequently, the genetic algorithm provides a flexible and powerful tool for traffic planning, allowing for customized solutions that meet predefined constraints while optimizing overall network performance. Imposing constraints also helps mitigate OOD issues by restricting the search space to feasible, realworld bounds. As a result, the genetic algorithm is less likely to generate extreme or unrealistic candidates that the machine-learning model cannot reliably evaluate. 

Fitness Score

In our experiments, we utilized two different fitness scores to evaluate and optimize our models. The first fitness function was the product of speed and flow, intended to maximize overall network throughput. This measure accounts for both traffic speed and volume, providing a more holistic proxy for network efficiency. The second fitness function considered flow only, with the goal of maximizing traffic throughput. To ensure that speed remained a crucial factor, we imposed a minimum-speed constraint derived from the HCM LOS criteria (Table 1). In our setting (FFS = 100 km/h), LOS A-C correspond to a minimum speed of 100 km/h; therefore, candidate solutions were required to maintain a predicted speed of at least 100 km/h. This constraint-based setup allowed us to explore the trade-off between maximizing throughput (flow) and maintaining acceptable operating speeds, providing a more robust evaluation of the proposed optimization strategy. 

EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION

PeMS Traffic Dataset

The dataset used in this study consists of historical traffic measurements collected from fixed loop detectors deployed along inter-urban freeway segments in the California Performance Measurement System (PeMS) (Chen et al., 2001), District 3. This district primarily covers dense urban and suburban regions in Northern California and provides high-resolution traffic observations across a large-scale road network. It includes over 1,000 monitored road segments, whose spatial distribution is illustrated in Figure 4. The data comprise traffic speed, flow, and occupancy measurements for each road segment, recorded at five-minute intervals, along with station-level metadata such as geographic coordinates and road direction. 

Each record in the dataset corresponds to a single measurement at a fixed station and time instant and includes a unique station identifier (Station ID), a precise timestamp (Timestamp), traffic flow measurements (Flow), representing the number of vehicles observed during the aggregation interval, and average traffic speed (Speed). In addition, the dataset contains static roadway attributes such as the number of lanes (Lanes) and the posted speed limit (max speed). To capture temporal dependencies, the raw measurements are augmented with lagged features of both flow and speed derived from previous time intervals. 

Prior to model training, an exploratory data anal-  To ensure data quality, stations with missing or invalid speed measurements due to sensor malfunction were excluded. Following this filtering process, 988 stations remained in the final dataset. The data were partitioned into training (60%), validation (10%), and test (30%) sets while preserving chronological order, as required for time-series modeling. All machine learning models were trained exclusively on the training set, with a held-out validation set used for hyperparameter tuning, early stopping and model selection. 

Traffic Prediction

In this subsection, we present results for our deeplearning spatio-temporal model for traffic speed prediction from traffic flow inputs. We evaluate performance against several baselines using three standard metrics that assess accuracy and robustness across temporal and spatial scales: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). MAE measures the average magnitude of prediction errors, RMSE places greater emphasis on larger errors by squaring them before averaging, and MAPE provides a scaleindependent percentage measure of prediction accuracy. 

Figure 7 shows the predicted speed and the actual speed for 4 roads from the road network using the LSTM model. 

Despite ST-GCNs' proven success in spatiotemporal prediction tasks, our results show that temporal models performed better in this case. While GNNs have demonstrated proficiency in time forecasting and exogenous regression for time series, the complexity of multivariate exogenous regression, specifically the interdependence of traffic flow and speed, may be too intricate for the current ST-GCN architecture. Incorporating additional components, such as attention mechanisms, may help address this limitation and improve performance. In future work, we plan to investigate such extensions to further enhance model accuracy. 

Genetic Algorithm-Based Flow Configuration Analysis

In this subsection, we present and analyze the results of our genetic algorithm-based approach for optimizing traffic flow across the network, focusing on its performance, consistency, and the impact of key algorithmic components. The deep learning model we incorporated in the genetic algorithm is the bestperforming model, the Bidirectional LSTM temporal model. To validate our approach and relate it to traditional guideline-based practice, we used the Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) LOS criteria as a source for a minimum-speed constraint. Specifically, for basic freeway segments with a free-flow speed (FFS) of 100 km/h (Table 1, Exhibit 23-2), the minimum speed for LOS A-C equals 100 km/h. We therefore enforced a minimum-speed threshold of 100 km/h, ensuring that the GA searches for flow configurations that preserve at least LOS C operating speeds under the learned flow-speed relationship. 

We conducted multiple independent runs of the genetic algorithm to assess the robustness and consistency of the results. Across these runs, the algorithm exhibited stable performance, indicating reliable convergence to consistent capacity-related solutions. Our evaluation focused on the speed proposed and flow proposed by the GA. 

Figure 8 compares, for each road segment, the GA-recommended flow distribution to the corresponding maximum (high-flow) levels. The histogram indicates that the proposed flows are systematically shifted toward lower values than the maximumflow baseline, reflecting the optimizer's tendency to regulate inflow in order to preserve feasible operating conditions rather than saturate the network. 

Figure 9 reports the corresponding speed distributions under three regimes: high-flow conditions, the GA-recommended flow configuration, and the average observed speed. As expected, speeds under high-flow conditions are concentrated at lower values, whereas the GA-recommended configuration yields a right-shifted distribution, indicating higher speeds. The proposed speeds typically lie between the highflow and average-speed baselines, suggesting that the GA improves speeds relative to congested conditions while remaining within realistic, data-consistent operating ranges. 

Discussion

Relative to guideline-based planning (HCM-style constraints), our approach offers several key advantages. First, whereas the HCM tables rely on fixed capacity values under idealized assumptions, the proposed genetic algorithm provides adaptive capacity estimation by dynamically adjusting flow recommendations according to current network conditions and the imposed constraints. 

In addition, the GA enables fine-grained optimization, producing more nuanced flow-speed combinations that can better exploit available capacity than the broader LOS-based categories typically used in the HCM framework. Importantly, the optimization process consistently satisfies the minimum-speed constraint derived from the HCM LOS criteria (Table 1), ensuring that the recommended flows preserve acceptable operating speeds. 

Finally, unlike HCM tables that are primarily applied at the level of individual segments, our method performs network-wide optimization, allowing coordinated flow adjustments across multiple links and thereby potentially improving overall system performance. 

CONCLUSION

Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating deep learning models with genetic algorithms for optimizing traffic flow and speed. By employing LSTM, Bidirectional LSTM networks and GNN for traffic speed prediction, and utilizing genetic algorithms for network-wide flow exploration under practical constraints, we illustrate the potential of combining deep learning with evolutionary optimization   as a data-driven complement to traditional guidelinebased approaches. Incorporating predicted speed into the fitness evaluation enables a more comprehensive and realistic assessment of candidate flow configurations, while also mitigating out-of-distribution effects during the optimization process. Based on our experiments, the Bidirectional LSTM (BiLSTM) achieves slightly better error metrics than the other evaluated models. We therefore use the trained BiLSTM in the subsequent optimization stage, where it serves as a fixed evaluation component for assessing candidate traffic flow configurations. 

The genetic algorithm yields feasible networkwide flow configurations that satisfy the minimumspeed constraints implied by the learned flow-speed relationship. By using the trained predictor as a fixed surrogate evaluator, the proposed framework offers a systematic way to define and assess performance criteria, enabling adaptive, fine-grained flow recommendations that go beyond the static, guideline-based capacity values implied by HCM. Across repeated runs, the GA consistently converges to high-quality solutions that respect operational constraints (e.g., minimum-speed requirements) while improving the speed-flow trade-off relative to unconstrained highflow conditions. 

In future work, to enable direct assessment of solution quality, we plan to incorporate traffic simulation environments with demand patterns that mimic real data. We will compare alternative optimizers, including gradient-based methods and classical capacity-planning formulations based on linear or nonlinear programming. Benchmarking these approaches alongside the proposed genetic algorithm under identical simulation conditions will clarify trade-offs among global search capability, computational efficiency, and solution quality, and help identify regimes, particularly high-dimensional, nonconvex settings, where evolutionary optimization offers clear advantages over more structured methods.

title: Intrathecal Delivery of BDNF into the Lumbar Cistern Re-Engages Locomotor Stepping after Spinal Cord Injury

body.text:
I. INTRODUCTION

S PINAL cord injury (SCI) leads to a loss of motor and sensory functions below the level of the lesion. Nonetheless, the intrinsic circuitry below the injury, in particular the locomotor circuitry, remains functional after complete isolation [4]. This is evidenced by the possibility of re-engaging the lumbar locomotor circuits through treadmill training to produce functional stepping in animal models of SCI [5]- [8]. Rehabilitative strategies using body weight supported training (BWST) are used clinically to improve stepping in spinal cord injured individuals. However, significant improvements have been observed only in patients with incomplete deficits (American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) C or D) [9]- [11]. Therefore, there is a need to identify different approaches to restore the functionality of the spinal circuitry. Neurotrophic factors, such as brain-derived neurotrophic factors (BDNF) and neurotrophin-3 (NT-3), are potential locomotion promoters as they are upregulated by intense exercise in both the spinal cord and hindlimb muscles [12] and associated with locomotor recovery [13]. We use delivery of neurotrophins to the spinal injury site to promote locomotor recovery comparable that observed with treadmill training, or supplement the recovery obtained with training [3]. Transplantation of fibroblasts engineered to express BDNF and/or NT-3 at the injury site of adult spinal cats can independently promote recovery of stepping in untrained animals, and the recovery is maintained up to 12 weeks after grafting [3], [14], [15].

Chronic intrathecal infusion of BDNF to the injury site through implantable osmotic pump was investigated as an axonal regeneration approach and found to enhance locomotor behavior [13]. Intrathecal delivery minimizes the risks of damage to the spinal cord as the associated surgery does not involve debriding scar tissue to create a pocket for the graft, or injections into the cord. The present work extends on the previous studies with intrathecal delivery by introducing the use of a programmable and implantable mini-pump for delivery of BDNF to the lumbar spinal cord, instead of at the injury site, in cats with complete thoracic SCI. Our results show that chronic intrathecal BDNF delivery promotes recovery of stepping ability in untrained spinalized cats as effectively as locomotor training and/or neurotrophin delivery at the injury site without causing additional damage to the cord. This delivery method is already largely accepted in clinical practice [16]- [18], overcomes the drawbacks associated with our previously used delivery methods, and is potentially clinically translational.

2.2-3.6 Kg). All animal care and procedures were performed according to the National Institute of Health guidelines, as well as to the USDA regulations for the use of felines in research and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Temple University (protocol 4272, initial approval 03/04/2016).

Animals were acclimated to walk on a motorized treadmill at a range of velocities between 0.3 and 0.8 m/s for up to 20 minutes/day for 3-8 weeks prior to spinal transection. Once acclimated, locomotor kinematics were collected, and the animals were spinalized. In eight cats, a 50 ng/day dose of BDNF was delivered intrathecally to the lumbar spinal cord for 35 days post-transection (post-Tx) through a programmable mini-pump implanted subdermally. The remaining six animals underwent spinal transection and catheter/pump implant as well, but the pump's reservoir was filled with 0.9% NaCl and those animals served as controls. Kinematic evaluation was conducted before, 3 and 5 weeks after injury/pump implant. Time points post-injury were chosen based on previous results with cellular delivery of neurotrophins into the transection cavity [14]. In six animals, four BDNF treated and two controls, Ground Reaction Forces (GRFs) were measured 5 weeks post-Tx during locomotion trials at 0.4 m/s to assess the animals' weight support ability. Animals were euthanized 5 weeks after injury and histological analysis was conducted.

B. Surgical Procedure: Spinal Transection and Pump Implant

Both spinal transection and pump implant took place during the same surgery, performed under aseptic conditions. Anesthesia was induced/maintained using isoflurane inhalation, and a midline incision was made between the T9 and L1 level. Muscles were detached from the dorsal aspect of the spinal column using a surgical spatula. Rongeurs were used to make a narrow laminectomy at the junction of the T11-T12 vertebrae. The dura was carefully opened and the spinal cord was severed between the T11-T12 roots with microscissor, leaving a 3-5 mm gap in the cord. The dura was sutured closed, then the muscles and finally the skin incision.

A second incision was then made between the L7 and S2 spinal segments. A catheter (32G, ReCathCo 220EO) was implanted within the lumbar cistern through the dura mater at the L7/S1 junction. The cannula was inserted subdurally and run rostrally until reaching approximately the L3 spinal segment level in two cats (BDNF-L3), while it was pushed until the L7 level in the other six cats (BDNF-L7). The catheter was then connected to a mini-pump (iPrecio SMP-200, MISZU, Tokyo) implanted subdermally. The pump was programmed to deliver a constant flow rate of 2 µL/h. The pump was filled with BDNF (Catalog#: H00000627-PO2, Abnova) diluted into 0.9% NaCl saline at a concentration of 1 µg/mL, thus delivering 50 ng/day of BDFN to the treated animal. Control animals underwent spinal transection and pump implant as well, but the pump was filled with 0.9% NaCl. The catheter was run subdurally to the L3 spinal segment in three of those animals and to the L7 spinal segment in the remaining three. The pump was refilled approximately every 15 days after implantation via percutaneous access to the pump's refill port.

C. Locomotor Training and Kinematic Data Collection

Cats were acclimated to a motorized treadmill through 20 minutes/day sessions of quadrupedal walking at a range of speed between 0.3 and 0.8 m/s prior to spinalization. The treadmill was enclosed in a Plexiglass frame to minimize lateral movements of the animals during training, and food rewards were given to entice the animal to walk forward. After transection, the forelimbs were kept stationary on a Plexiglas platform elevated 1 cm above the treadmill and a Plexiglas divider was placed between the hindlimbs to avoid scissoring of the limbs during bipedal hindlimb locomotion.

Locomotion was recorded using the Vicon motion capture system (Vicon Motion System Ltd., Oxford, UK). Three infrared cameras collected the positions of 11 reflective markers placed on the cat skin at the level of the ischium, femoral head, knee joint, lateral malleolus, metatarsophalangeal joint and the tip of the digits on the right hindlimb as well as on the humeral head, elbow joint lateral epicondyle, metacarpophalangeal joint and the tip of the digits on the right forelimb. Fig. 1 shows the location of the reflective markers. After injury, the experimenter (MAL) held the cat at the base of the tail to provide balance support during locomotor sessions and perineal stimulation was delivered to maximize locomotor output in each of the animals [3], [14], [15]. Only perineal stimulation sufficient to initiate/maintain stepping was applied, as excessive stimulation can interrupt stepping or cause aberrant patterns. Actual treadmill recording time was approximately 1 minute at each speed, a time duration that has shown no training effects in previous studies in our laboratory [3]. Animal's gait kinematics were evaluated, and the animal was considered able to step when capable of executing 10 consecutive plantar weight bearing steps after injury at the speed tested, and all the speeds below.

D. Kinematic Analysis

Horizontal and vertical components of each joint marker were exported and processed using custom Matlab (Mathworks, Naticik, MA) scripts. The slippage of the knee and elbow markers was corrected by triangulating their positions from the neighboring markers and bone segment lengths, obtained post-mortem [19]. Quantitative analysis of the stepping parameters was conducted with IgorPro (Wavemetrics, Lake Oswego, OR) and then exported to SPSS (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL) for statistical evaluation.

Marker locations were used to calculate a number of kinematic parameters, which included: stance length, swing height, Da (horizontal displacement of the foot relative to hip at toedown), Dp (horizontal displacement of the foot relative to hip at liftoff), and hindlimb joint angles excursion. Values of stance length, swing height, Da, Dp were normalized to pretransection values.

Kinematic parameters were exported to SPSS (IBM Corp., Armonk NY) for statistical analysis. The average values of each parameter per trial (i.e. about 60 sec of walking) was calculated in order to reduce the number of data points. To evaluate the effects of BDNF delivery on the amount of locomotor recovery, linear mixed models with the kinematic parameters (stance length, swing height, etc.) as the dependent variable and speed (0.4 & 0.8 m/s) and time postimplant (3 & 5 wks) as repeated measure factors were used to evaluate the effects of those factors on the kinematic parameters. The estimated marginal means (EMMs) of the dependent variables were then compared to 100% (i.e. pretransection level). Linear mixed models were also used to evaluate the effects of time (before, 3 and 5 weeks after injury; time as a repeated measure factor) on joints angles for the BDNF group. Post-hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction between the means at the different times were then conducted.

E. Ground Reaction Forces Data Collection and Analysis

Ground reaction forces (GRFs) were collected in six cats (two Controls and four BDNFs) during locomotion trials 5 weeks post-transection using an instrumented split belt treadmill where each belt motor assembly (left and right) was mounted on a Kistler force plate (Kistler Instrument Corp., Winterhur, SUI) [20]. The vertical components of the GRFs (Fz) were evaluated during locomotion at 0.4 m/s to estimate the animals' ability to weight support. Stepping during locomotion trials was initiated, and when necessary maintained, via perineal stimulation. Forces applied to the tail were minimized during those trials and the animal was allowed to drop as low as possible while maintaining the locomotor cycle. The vertical force components under the right and left hind paws were evaluated. Data were collected at 960 Hz and processed in Matlab (The Mathworks, Natick, MA) using customized scripts.

Values of the vertical component of the force (Fz) in Volts were first converted into Newton using the manufacturer's conversion factor (5 mV/N). A Butterworth filter with cut-off frequency of 10 Hz was applied to remove vibration associated noise from the locomotion data. The peak vertical forces were evaluated and averaged for each trial and then normalized for the cats' weight at the time of the recording session. For the BDNF cats, we set a threshold of 2 N/kg, in order to keep only valid peaks not biased by the animal's position being re-adjusted on the treadmill. The value of the threshold was lowered to 1 N/kg for Control cats, since this group showed only few or no force peaks higher than 2 N/kg. A linear mixed model with average peak vertical force per trial as the dependent variable and group (BDNF or Control), side (left or right) and the group * side interaction as factors (with side and trial as repeated measure variables and cat as the grouping variable) was used to evaluate the effects of group on the peak vertical GRF. According to results on able-bodied cats showing that the hindlimbs support about 40% of the body weight during locomotion [21], [22], the vertical force necessary for full weight support is about 4 N/kg (normalized to the animal's mass) [20].

F. Tissue Preparation and Histological Procedures

At the conclusion of the experiment, animals were euthanized and intracardially perfused with 0.9% cold saline flush followed by cold 4% paraformaldehyde in phosphate buffer. After fixation of the tissue, the thoracic and lumbar spinal cord were carefully retrieved and post-fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde. After 2-3 weeks, the tissue was then cryoprotected in 30% sucrose solution for at least one week. The spinal cord was then divided into small segments, usually < 1 cm, embedded in M-1 matrix medium, and frozen at −80 • C. Frozen tissues were cut into 40 µm thick horizontal sections on a cryostat, mounted on charged glass slides and kept at −20 • C until immunohistochemistry and staining were performed.

To investigate the potential trauma caused by catheter insertion, we stained for Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP). Staining was performed on eight animals: five BDNF (two with L3 delivery and three with L7 delivery) and three Control (two with L3 delivery and one with L7 delivery) on horizontal sections taken from the catheter entry zone's segment (L7/S1) to the segment where the tip of the catheter was found postmortem. Since the glial scar formed at the lesion site after SCI is populated with reactive astrocytes which undergo morphological changes and increase synthesis of GFAP, we stained the transection site of four cats (three BDNF and one Control) to serve as reference.

Horizontal sections were left at room temperature for 10-15 minutes and tissue was surrounded with hydrophobic pen. Sections were rehydrated with three 5-minutes rinses in PBS and blocked with 5% NGS in dilution buffer for one hour at room temperature. The dilution buffer included Tris-HCl pH 7.2 (25 mM), NaCl (300 mM), 0.3% Triton X-100, BSA (0.5 mg/ml) and 0.01% Thimerosal diluted in 100 ml PBS. Tissues were then incubated in primary antibody in buffer solution overnight at 4 • C (1:500, Polyclonal rabbit antibody Anti-GFAP, Dako). Lesion completeness was visually confirmed in all cats and histologically verified using Nissl-myelin staining in a subset of animals. The Luxol Fast Blue Stain (Myelin Stain) from Abcam was used to identify the basic neuronal structure in the spinal cord. Staining was performed on five cats and the chosen sections were distributed over different depth levels of the spinal cord in order to evaluate lesion completeness over the entire thickness of the cord. Fig. 2 illustrates the kinematics of the right hindlimb for one exemplar step during locomotion before and after injury for one animal in each group. BDNF treated animals recovered plantar weight-bearing stepping, while saline treated animals stepped mostly on the dorsal aspect of the paw. Five BDNF cats were capable of executing 10 consecutive plantar weightbearing steps at 0.4 m/s as early as 3 weeks post-Tx; and among them, three had recovered stepping abilities for the full range of velocities tested (0.3-0.8 m/s) by that time. By 5 weeks, five could step at all the velocities tested, one could step at up to 0.5 m/s and two did not step at any walking speed. The pump's reservoir leaked subdermally in one of those two animals, leading to pump encapsulation. In the second cat, histology analysis did not show BDNF accumulation meaningfully higher than background level within the cord's tissue, suggesting that either the delivered protein was not active or did not infuse intrathecally.

III. RESULTS

A. Overall Kinematic Observations

Although two Control cats could perform some stepping at slow velocities (0.3-0.4 m/s), all but one never executed 10 consecutive weight-bearing plantar steps at any of the speeds tested and showed mostly dorsal foot placement during stance. Overall, the proportion of animals who recovered stepping ability up to at least 0.4 m/s at 5 weeks was significantly higher in BDNF treated animal (6/7 (excluding leaking pump case) versus 1/6 in Control (Fischer's Exact Test, p =.016).

Lesion completeness was confirmed by Nissl-myelin stain of the transection site in the one Control cat that could step so the recovery can not be attributed to a partial injury. Despite recent claims of spontaneous locomotor recovery in spinal cats [23], we [3], [14], and others [2], [7], [8], have never observed such a level of spontaneous recovery in untrained spinalized cats, and the animal was considered an outlier and excluded from further analysis.

B. Kinematic Parameters

Kinematic parameters were evaluated in the six BDNF treated cats that could step at up to 0.5 m/s by 5 weeks post-Tx via the use of linear mixed models. In BDNF treated cats, time post-Tx had a significant effect on stance length (p = .002), swing height (p = .015), Da (p = .002) and Dp (p = .049) while speed and the speed * time interaction term had no effect (p > .05, range .094-.7390). BDNF treated cats showed post-Tx values of stance length and swing height comparable to pre-transection levels. EMMs of the stance length and swing height indices for the BDNF cats are shown in Figs. 3A and B for the 3 and 5 weeks post-injury time points while walking at medium (0.4 m/s) or maximum velocity (0.8 m/s). Controls were incapable of reaching the minimum of 10 consecutive plantar steps and, thus, statistical evaluation was not performed on this group. In contrast, BDNF treated animals recovered 75±18% (mean ±95%CI (confidence interval)) of their stance length when walking at medium speed (0.4 m/s) 5 weeks post-Tx. Similarly, they recovered 78±18% of pre-transection values at the maximum walking speed tested (0.8 m/s), but in both cases the values were significantly lower than the pretransection values (95% CI of the EMMs did not include 100%). Swing height index post-Tx was 88±18% of pretransection value while stepping at 0.4 m/s and 73±20% of pre-transection value while stepping at 0.8 m/s. Animals recovered swing height to pre-transection value when walking at 0.4 m/s, but they showed a statistically lower swing height when walking at 0.8 m/s (EMM 95% CI did not include 100%). When compared to previous studies with treadmill training or cellular delivery at the transection site [1][2][3]14], our results suggest that intrathecal delivery of BDNF to the lumbar spinal cord is as efficacious as training or BDNF cellular delivery at the injury site at promoting the recovery of locomotor behavior in untrained spinalized cats.

Data for Da and Dp indices are shown in Figs. 3C and D. All BDNF treated cats showed decreased Da and increased Dp 3 weeks post-injury. E. Histological Analysis

After sacrifice, the cord was retrieved from each animal. Gross examination of the spinal cord did not show any damage due to catheter insertion. The GFAP staining confirmed this result, underlining the safety of intrathecal BDNF delivery through implantable mini-pump. We compared the catheter insertion area, L7 for the BDNFs-L7 group and from L7 to L3 for the BDNFs-L3 group, to the transection site, which served as our control. As expected, high GFAP expression, was found in the tissue surrounding the transection lesion. No significant accumulation above background levels was observed at the cannula insertion area as well as in the cord from the entry point to the site of BDNF delivery, indicating minimal catheter-associated trauma (Fig. 6).

Transection sections were stained with Nissl-myelin to assess the completeness of the injury and potential growth across the lesion. As previously shown, [3], [14], no axonal regeneration was detected across the lesion, indicating that the lesion was complete.

IV. DISCUSSION

This is the first study to report locomotor recovery using intrathecal delivery of BDNF to the lumbar spinal cord via a programmable and implantable mini-pump in a feline spinal cord transection injury model.

The major findings of this study are 1) intrathecal delivery of BDNF to the lumbar spinal cord promotes the recovery of locomotor behavior in untrained spinalized cats that is 2) similar or better than the recovery obtained with cellular delivery at the transection site, 3) delivery via implantable and programmable mini-pump is a safe method for complete spinal cord injury treatment, posing minimal risk to the animals and their spinal cord.

A. Advantages of Intrathecal BDNF Delivery via Implantable Mini-Pump

This study showed that BDNF treated cats could step at all range of velocities tested (0.3-0.8 m/s), as early as 3 weeks post injury, and that stepping was maintained for the entire duration of the experiment (5 weeks post-Tx). Intrathecal delivery of BDNF was as effective as delivery via cellular grafts or treadmill training alone in our model at restoring locomotor functions. This was underlined by the similar or better recovery of stance length and swing height compared to data previously reported with NTF grafts implanted at the injury site or locomotor training [1]- [3], [14].

Kinematic analysis shows similar gait recovery with BDNF or treadmill training in spinalized cats. The analysis of the GRFs also showed results similar to trained animals in terms of weight support [20] and superior to non-treated animals. The BDNF treated cats were capable of performing some full weight-bearing stepping during locomotion at medium speed (0.4 m/s). The statistically significant differences with the minimal force required for full weight bearing in ablebodied cats (4 N/kg) may in part be due to a different weight distribution between fore-and hind-limbs in spinal cats. The hindlimbs weight loss resulting from muscles atrophy may reduce the minimum force necessary for full weight bearing, allowing BDNF treated cats to achieve full weigh support even at lower forces. Control cats that received saline were incapable of plantar weight-bearing stepping on a consistent basis.

While delivery of neurotrophin producing grafts promoted locomotor recovery, it required an invasive surgery that produces additional damage to the spinal cord and the neurotrophin delivery level is neither constant nor controlled. Those drawbacks represent significant obstacles for clinical application. The features of the micro infusion pump, such as being programmable, subdermally implantable and percutaneously refillable, minimize the number of invasive surgeries and allow delivery of a constant and controlled dosage of Fig. 6. Fibroblasts engineered to produce BDNF produced different levels of BDNF, all leading to similar levels of locomotor performances [3], but their production was downgraded by 5 weeks post-grafting [14]. Those results suggest that the dose range effective at promoting locomotor recovery may be relatively large and that delivery may not need to be continuous. In this study, the use of an implantable and programmable mini-pump allowed delivery of a controlled dosage and the determination of a minimum effective dosage of BDNF necessary to elicit locomotor recovery. This is important for defining standardized protocols for SCI treatment. We delivered a significantly lower dosage of protein (50 ng/day) compared to previous studies (150 µg/day in [13]), which most likely eliminated the synchronous hindlimb activity observed with viral delivery where dosage is difficult to control [24], [25]. Future studies covering a greater range of dosage may uncover a dosing range that would lead to recovery of stepping at all speeds tested in all BDNF treated animals, yet avoid spastic-like hindlimb movements. This dosage may be species-specific but it would still provide valuable information about potential clinical outcomes if BDNF treatment is attempted in humans.

B. Implantable and Programmable Mini-Pump Is a Safe Method for Intrathecal BDNF Delivery

Prior results suggests that intrathecal BDNF delivery in humans would be a safe approach that could obtain FDA approval for clinical tests. Chronic intrathecal infusion has been proven safe and effective for Baclofen delivery for spasticity treatment [17] and morphine delivery for pain treatment [18] in clinical trials. Mechanical complications (catheter or pump issues [26]- [28]; similar to our leakage problem in one cat) have been observed in a number of cases and required revisions but can be reduced with appropriate techniques and post-surgical management [29]. Lumbar intrathecal pump delivery has also been used in Phase I/II clinical trials for BDNF delivery in ALS patients receiving a range of dosing: 25, 60, 150, 400, and 1000 µg/day [16]. Patients reported events of minor severity due to pump/catheter implant that mainly consisted of post-surgical headache and local pain [16]. In line with these results in humans, gross examination of the animals' spinal cord retrieved at 5 weeks post-injury showed no damage to the cord or roots. Delivery to the lower lumbar cisterna is minimally invasive and the additional intrathecal space at that level reduces the risk of potential damage to the spinal cord. GFAP stain confirmed the visual and microscopic examination results, showing minimal trauma and inflammation due to catheter insertion and establishing the safety of the delivery method.

C. Regeneration Is an Unlikely Mechanism for Locomotor Recovery

As previously reported in [3], [14], [15], Nissl-myelin stain showed no axonal regeneration across the lesion cavity, confirming that locomotor recovery is not associated with axonal regeneration. Prior reports on delivery of BDNF to the spinal injury site concentrated on the effects of neurotrophins on axonal growth and sprouting to promote recovery of function [13], [30]- [32]. These studies showed the benefits of exogenously applied neurotrophic factors to axonal regrowth in mature neurons [33], [34] but while increased axonal regrowth was seen within the lesion and the cord caudal to the lesion, few axons extended beyond the injury site [13], [35]. In our study, since locomotor recovery occurred as early as 3 weeks after injury and was not associated with any axonal sprouting across the lesion site, regeneration of descending axons is an unlikely mechanism for recovery in BDNF treated cats. We instead propose that locomotor recovery can be attributed to the BDNF-induced plasticity within the lumbar spinal cord. We can speculate that the mechanism by which this class of NTFs induces recovery may be similar to the mechanism by which BWS training promotes locomotor activity. As previously shown by Gomez-Pinilla et al., exercise induces up-regulation of BDNF mRNA in the lumbar spinal neurons and skeletal muscles of complete spinalized rats [12]. In particular, studies have shown that, unlike other classes of neurotrophins, BDNF is released in an activity-dependent manner and exercise intensity modulates serum BDNF concentrations [36], [37]. It is likely that exogenous delivery of BDNF mirrors the increase in BDNF that results from training and exercise, activating the same mechanisms. Neurotrophins have been shown to contribute to the efficiency of synaptic transmission [38], and produce an increase in the expression levels of molecules involved in neurotransmission [25] when delivered to the spinal cord. Changes in spinal synaptic transmission following training have been directly implicated in recovery of stepping [39], [40] and simulation studies with a basic neuromechanical model of the cat limb have shown that increases in synaptic strength like the ones seen with delivery of neurotrophins or locomotor training are sufficient to restore locomotor capabilities [41], [42]. Furthermore, electrophysiological studies conducted by Mendell's group showed that chronic BDNF or NT-3 delivery quickly enhances functional connectivity to motoneuron in the neonatal rat, and it does it as early as after 6 hours of treatment [43]- [45]. Thus, the strengthening of synaptic connections between the interneurons of the lumbar spinal cord remains a likely potential mechanism by which NTFs restore locomotion in animal models of complete SCI.
